lessons.unit: Unit 1B: Anthology poetry (16 poems) - comparison skills
lessons.title: Comparing poems: voice and perspective (If- and Prayer Before Birth)
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a poet's choice of speaker change what a poem can say?
objectives: Explain the Section B task: compare two anthology poems for AO2 (methods) and AO3 (links)
Use a four-part comparison paragraph: point, evidence, zoom, link
Compare the voices in If- and Prayer Before Birth
successCriteria: All: identify who speaks and who is addressed in each poem
Most: write a comparison paragraph with a linking connective
Some: compare how form and structure shape each voice
lessons.crossCurricular: English Language: voice, tone and perspective in non-fiction and fiction writing
lessons.smsc: Moral: what makes a person steady and trustworthy; Social: responsibility towards the next generation

keywords.def: the speaker or persona who 'talks' in a poem
the viewpoint from which something is presented
repeating a word or phrase at the start of successive lines
to set two things side by side and discuss similarities and differences
the attitude or mood the writer creates

starter: Bismillah. Section B is worth 30 marks. Which two assessment objectives does it assess?
Define 'imagery' and give one example from any poem you know.
Name three things you must say about a poem's voice (who, to whom, how).

teach.heading: The Section B task
bullets: Part 3 of the Pearson anthology: 16 poems, all studied
One 30-mark question, a choice of two
Questions ask you to compare two poems
About 40 minutes; a clean copy of the poems is supplied
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Explain that the exam supplies the poems, so we never memorise long quotations: we learn short flexible phrases and, above all, a method. AO2 is language, form and structure; AO3 is links and connections between texts. Say plainly that the question wording on the live paper must be checked against the latest past papers, and share the 2025 examiners' report wording with the class when available. TEACHER: supply If- (Kipling) and Prayer Before Birth (MacNeice) from the school's licensed copy of the anthology.

teach.heading: Who speaks, and to whom?
teach.note: Pupils annotate both poems for speaker and addressee. If-: an older, authoritative voice advising a son, with the 'then' (the reward) held back until the last two lines of the final stanza. Prayer Before Birth: the voice of an unborn child pleading with God (and the world) for protection, in a litany of requests that closes with the stark 'Otherwise kill me.' Ask: who holds the power in each poem? Likely answer: the adult in If-, nobody (the child is powerless) in Prayer. Context, briefly: If- was published in 1910 and reflects Victorian and Edwardian ideals of self-control and duty; Prayer Before Birth dates from the Second World War, when MacNeice feared a world that crushes the individual.

left.title: If- (Kipling)
points: Long chain of conditions: 'If you can...'

teach.heading: Model: one comparison paragraph
teach.note: I do. Read the model aloud, then colour-code the four parts with the class (point, evidence, zoom, link). Stress that the link sentence is where AO3 marks are earned and that connectives such as 'whereas', 'similarly', 'in contrast' do real work. Check that pupils see the quotations are short and embedded in the sentence.

model.problem: Compare how the speakers' voices are presented in If- and Prayer Before Birth.
steps: Point: both poets give the speaker a repeated pattern, but for opposite purposes.
Evidence: Kipling opens line after line with 'If', MacNeice repeats 'I am not yet born'.
Zoom: the conditional 'If' makes the advice sound like a test of character the son must pass, while the child's repeated statement stresses helplessness: it has no life yet and no power.
Link: whereas Kipling's anaphora builds towards a confident reward, MacNeice's builds towards the desperate 'Otherwise kill me.'
model.answer: Both poets use repetition to shape the voice, but for contrasting effects. Kipling's repeated 'If' makes the speaker sound like an assured father setting out a test of character, whereas MacNeice's repeated 'I am not yet born' stresses the speaker's helplessness. In If- the pattern builds towards a reward, while in Prayer Before Birth it builds towards the desperate 'Otherwise kill me.'

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. Reveal the answer after everyone has voted. The trap in B is that it makes a point about one poem only: this is the classic 'two separate essays' weakness. A names a technique but not an effect.

check.q: Which sentence best earns AO3 marks?
options: Kipling uses repetition of 'If'.
Kipling's voice is confident, whereas MacNeice's speaker is powerless, as the repeated 'I am not yet born' shows.
MacNeice wrote his poem during the Second World War.
Both poems are good poems about people.
check.why: Only B links the two poems and explains the effect with a short quotation. A is one-poem technique spotting, C is context without analysis, D is vague.

teach.heading: Form and structure link-ups
bullets: If-: four stanzas, one long build-up
Prayer: a series of pleas, stanza by stanza
Ask: what does each ending leave us feeling?
Structure is also AO2: comment on it every time
teach.note: Pupils often skip structure. Ask where each poem ends and why that matters: If- ends on its promise ('you'll be a Man, my son'), Prayer Before Birth ends on a threat to the listener. Encourage pupils to say what the order of ideas does to the reader. Misconception to correct: structure is not just 'it has four stanzas'; it is the shape of the whole poem and the effect of the shape.

practice: As a class, annotate If- for every use of 'you' and 'your'. What relationship does this create with the reader?
In pairs, find two short phrases from Prayer Before Birth that show fear. Write a one-sentence effect for each.
Join this sentence with a connective: 'Kipling's speaker is confident. MacNeice's speaker is vulnerable.'
independent: Core: write one comparison paragraph (point, evidence, zoom, link) on voice in the two poems, using the model structure.
Extend: add a second paragraph comparing how each poem ends.
Stretch: write a paragraph on how the historical context of 1910 and 1942 explains the different voices, without bolting on facts.
exit: Who is the speaker in each poem?
Write one linking sentence using 'whereas' or 'similarly'.
Return to the big question: how does a poet's choice of speaker change what a poem can say?
lessons.homework: Write a 120-word comparison paragraph on the tone of the two poems. Use two short quotations.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a sentence-starter bank (Both poets... whereas... this suggests...) and a glossary of 'litany', 'conditional', 'plea' with first-language notes. Stretch: pupils consider whether Kipling's confidence could be read ironically.

lessons.title: Blessing: imagery, voice and community
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a poet turn a moment of scarcity into a moment of grace?
objectives: Analyse how Dharker presents water, scarcity and joy
Explain the effect of religious and violent imagery
Plan a paragraph on language and structure
successCriteria: All: identify imagery of water and of thirst
Most: explain effects of three images
Some: link the poem's movement from scarcity to abundance to its form and voice
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: water scarcity and access; PSHE: community and fairness
lessons.smsc: Social: sharing resources; Spiritual: gratitude and mercy (rahmah) as human values

keywords.def: descriptive language that appeals to the senses
a comparison using 'like' or 'as'
saying one thing is another
a group of words linked by meaning
placing contrasting ideas together

starter: Bismillah. Name four types of imagery (e.g. visual, auditory).
Define 'simile' and 'metaphor' with one original example each.
Why does the poet's choice of verbs matter more than adjectives in many poems?

teach.heading: What is the poem about?
bullets: A water pipe bursts in a poor community
People rush to the water; the moment is joyful
The poem moves from thirst to overflowing
Dharker (born in Pakistan, raised in Glasgow) writes of India
teach.note: TEACHER: supply Blessing (Imtiaz Dharker) from the school's licensed anthology. Read it aloud once without comment. Ask pupils for a one-sentence summary before analysis. Context: Dharker's poems often explore communities in South Asia and the tension between hardship and dignity. Do not overstate: the poem does not name a particular place, so avoid claiming a specific town.

teach.heading: Scarcity and abundance in language
teach.note: Pupils sort words and phrases from the poem into two columns. Dharker begins with a harsh sense of thirst (the cracking, drying skin of the opening) and ends with an excess of water. Draw attention to the fact that the language of lack is physical and painful, while the language of plenty is noisy and joyful. This contrast is the poem's structure.

left.title: Language of scarcity
points: A sense of waiting for 'a kind god'

teach.heading: Model: analysing a short phrase
teach.note: I do. Model aloud the thinking: what is the image, what does it make us see or feel, why this word, what bigger idea? Point out that the answer comes from one or two words (the verb 'crashes', the metaphor of silver), not from retelling.

model.problem: Analyse how Dharker presents the water as precious.
steps: Point: the water is presented as a kind of treasure.
Evidence: it is likened to 'silver'.
Zoom: the metaphor links water to wealth, suggesting that in a place of drought it is worth more than money; the verb 'crashes' gives it force and noise.
Link: this prepares for the idea of divine generosity (a 'blessing') in the title.
model.answer: Dharker presents the water as precious by comparing it to silver. The metaphor suggests a treasure that is rare and valuable, which makes sense in a community that has little, while the forceful verb 'crashes' adds noise and energy, as if the gift cannot be contained. The image supports the title, since the water seems to be a gift from beyond human control.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Use mini-whiteboards. Discuss the wrong answers: pupils often say the poem is 'about a flood'. The key is that a burst pipe in a place of scarcity is received as a gift.

check.q: What is the best reading of the title 'Blessing'?
options: The poem is about a religious ceremony.
A burst pipe, usually a problem, is welcomed as a gift in a place of scarcity.
The poet is blessing the water company.
The poem is about a flood that destroys a village.
check.why: The title is ironic and affirming: something that would be a nuisance elsewhere becomes a gift here. A and D misread the scene; C is invented.

teach.heading: Voice and structure
bullets: Who sees and narrates the scene?
Note how the poem moves in time
Where does the mood turn?
Free verse: why avoid a regular pattern?
teach.note: Ask pupils to consider the effect of free verse: the lines can rush, like the water. Ask where the mood lifts and how line length helps. Remind them AO2 includes structure, so one structural comment is expected in every response.

practice: As a class, find three verbs of movement in the poem and rank them by intensity.
Write one sentence explaining why a simile might be weaker than a metaphor for a miracle.
Pair talk: whose point of view do we see in the poem, and does it change?
independent: Core: write a paragraph analysing one image of scarcity and one of abundance.
Extend: write about how the poet's use of religious language shapes our sense of the event.
Stretch: plan a comparison paragraph between Blessing and one other poem about community (choose from the anthology).
exit: Name one image of scarcity from the poem.
Name one image of abundance.
Big question: how does the poet turn a moment of scarcity into a moment of grace?
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph (about 100 words) on how the final stanza makes the reader feel. Use one short quotation.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a word bank of sensory vocabulary (dry, rush, crash, flood) with pictures. EAL pupils can add a first-language word for 'blessing'. Stretch: explore how the poem avoids sentimentality.

lessons.title: Search For My Tongue: language, identity and the body
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens to a person's identity when they live between two languages?
objectives: Explain how Bhatt uses the tongue as a symbol of language and identity
Analyse the effect of the shifts between English and Gujarati
Link structure to the speaker's journey
successCriteria: All: explain what 'tongue' means in the poem
Most: analyse an extended metaphor and a shift of language
Some: evaluate how form mirrors identity
lessons.crossCurricular: Arabic: language, translation and identity; Geography: migration
lessons.smsc: Cultural: valuing mother tongues and heritage; Social: belonging

keywords.def: a comparison that runs through a section or the whole poem
something that stands for a bigger idea
able to speak two languages
the first language a person learns
a section written as a dream, often to show the unconscious

starter: Bismillah. What does AO2 reward?
Define 'extended metaphor'.
Which two meanings can the word 'tongue' have?

teach.heading: The poem's idea
bullets: The speaker lives in an English-speaking country
She fears losing her mother tongue
The tongue is both language and body part
The poem ends with the mother tongue returning
teach.note: TEACHER: supply Search For My Tongue (Sujata Bhatt) from the school's licensed anthology. Bhatt, born in India, writes about her Gujarati mother tongue and English. The poem includes lines in Gujarati and a transliteration, which pupils may find striking. Do not claim details of Gujarati vocabulary beyond what is printed. EAL pupils with a second language may offer their own insights: invite them, but never put anyone on the spot.

teach.heading: Tongue as body and language
teach.note: Ask: why a body part? A tongue tastes, speaks, is physical. The poem pushes the physical and the cultural together. Use the compare block to sort pupils' ideas.

left.title: Tongue as the body
points: Physical, can be cut or grow back

right.title: Tongue as language
points: Mother tongue stays in the mouth

teach.heading: Model: analysing language and form
teach.note: I do. Emphasise explanation of the symbolism, not just 'it is a metaphor'. Ask: what would be lost if the poem were entirely in English?

model.problem: How does Bhatt show the speaker's fear of losing her language?
steps: Point: she presents language as a body part that could be lost.
Evidence: she says she has 'lost my tongue'.
Zoom: the verb 'lose' suggests carelessness or accident, but the body image makes it feel like a painful operation, which shows how much the loss would hurt her sense of self.
Link: the later image of the tongue growing back shows hope and resilience.
model.answer: Bhatt presents language as a part of the body that can be lost. The idea of losing a 'tongue' suggests an accidental, painful removal, and therefore shows that language is not a skill she can set aside but a part of her identity. This makes the later image of regrowth hopeful and powerful.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: A common misconception is that the poem is about being forced to give up the language. It is more about the quiet threat of forgetting it in a different country.

check.q: Why might Bhatt include lines in Gujarati?
options: To show off her language skills.
To make the reader experience the mother tongue as a presence in the poem.
Because the poem is a translation.
To make the poem harder for English readers.
check.why: The Gujarati is part of the meaning: the mother tongue literally appears on the page, which the speaker feels she may lose. A, C and D miss the effect.

teach.heading: Structure: a journey in the poem
bullets: Opening: the fear of losing the tongue
Middle: a dream-like, growing image
End: reassurance and reclamation
Notice the shift in tone as the poem develops
teach.note: Ask where the turn is and what pushes it. Pupils should treat the dream-like stage as the poem's heart. Link to Half-caste (poem 14): both deal with identity and voice, a link we will return to for comparison. AO3: always link, but compare methods as well as ideas.

practice: Retrieve: list three techniques from this term and an effect for each.
Why might a poet choose a body image for a language?
In pairs, explain the phrase 'mother tongue' to someone who does not know it.
independent: Core: write a paragraph on how the tongue is used as a symbol.
Extend: add a paragraph on the effect of the Gujarati lines.
Stretch: write a plan for comparing Search For My Tongue with another poem about identity.
exit: Name two meanings of 'tongue'.
How does the poem end in tone?
Big question: what happens to identity between two languages?
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph on the poem's ending. What does the speaker feel about her language by the close?
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a bilingual glossary (tongue, mother tongue, heritage) and sentence stems. EAL pupils may read the poem aloud in their home language for comparison of sound. Stretch: explore the ethics of translation in poetry.

lessons.title: Childhood and memory: Piano, Half-past Two and Hide and Seek
lessons.bigQuestion: How do poets use a child's point of view, or a memory of childhood, to shape feeling?
objectives: Analyse how Lawrence uses memory in Piano
Apply the voice-and-perspective method to Half-past Two and Hide and Seek
Compare adult and child perspectives
successCriteria: All: summarise each poem's situation
Most: analyse one phrase from Piano in detail
Some: compare the child's world in two poems
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: memory and growing up
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: gratitude for childhood and family; Moral: kindness to children

keywords.def: a sentimental longing for the past
a viewpoint that sees the world as a child would
two consecutive lines that rhyme
repeated 's' sounds
a pull between two feelings or ideas

starter: Bismillah. What is the difference between tone and mood?
Define 'enjambment'.
Why might a poem about childhood use short sentences?

teach.heading: Piano: the pull of the past
bullets: A woman singing softly stirs a memory
The speaker recalls sitting under a piano
The adult present resists the childhood past
Lawrence (1885-1930) writes in regular quatrains
teach.note: TEACHER: supply Piano (D H Lawrence) from the school's licensed anthology. Piano is safe to analyse in detail. The speaker is taken back by the singer's voice to his childhood and his mother's presence at the piano; the pull of nostalgia is both sweet and painful. The poem ends with the grown man weeping 'like a child for the past'. Lawrence's poem has three stanzas, each a rhymed quatrain, a controlled structure that contrasts with the emotion bursting through it.

teach.heading: Model: tension in Piano
teach.note: I do. Model the thought process: spot the contrasting pair, explain each, then give the overall effect. Pupils must say what the quotation shows about the speaker's feelings.

model.problem: How does Lawrence present the tension between past and present in Piano?
steps: Point: he presents the past as sweet but the present as an emotional intrusion.
Evidence: the tune is 'tinkling', while the grown man weeps 'like a child'.
Zoom: 'tinkling' is light and delicate, suggesting childhood innocence; the weeping shows the adult is overwhelmed by loss.
Link: the regular rhyme tries to impose order, but the emotion breaks through.
model.answer: Lawrence presents the past as sweet and the present as emotionally overpowering. The 'tinkling' piano suggests a light, innocent childhood, whereas the adult's weeping 'like a child' shows how powerfully the memory overwhelms him. The regular rhyme scheme gives an appearance of control which the strength of feeling undermines.

teach.heading: Two poems, one method
bullets: Half-past Two (Fanthorpe): a child and the clock
Hide and Seek (Scannell): a boy hiding in a game
Apply: who speaks, who sees, what changes?
Teacher supplies both texts
teach.note: TEACHER: supply both poems from the school's licensed anthology. For these two poems the lesson is a method lesson: pupils apply the voice-and-perspective questions to the printed text. Do not rely on memory of the poems: read them aloud and have pupils annotate. Prompt questions: Who is the child? How does the poet signal the child's point of view (sentence length, vocabulary, play with words)? What does the child understand that the adult does not? What does the ending do? Link to the Year 10 context: Fanthorpe writes about time and misunderstanding in a school; Scannell about a child's game turning into isolation. Check these summaries against the text before teaching.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Quick vote. Ask pupils to defend B or D. D confuses form with meaning: regular form can carry strong emotion.

check.q: Which statement is the best analytical point about Piano?
options: The poem has three stanzas.
Lawrence contrasts a delicate, childlike past with an emotionally overwhelmed present.
Lawrence liked pianos.
The poem is about a woman who sings.
check.why: B states a meaning and contrast that can be supported with evidence. A is a feature without effect, C is a guess, D is a summary.

teach.heading: Comparing perspectives
teach.note: Use the table to plan for a comparison. Pupils add evidence from the texts after you supply them.

practice: Retrieve: name two ways poets show a child's voice.
Say aloud a childhood memory triggered by a sound or smell.
What does 'tension' mean in a poem?
independent: Core: write a paragraph on Piano using the model.
Extend: complete the table for the two supplied poems with a short quotation each.
Stretch: plan a comparison of the child's perspective in Half-past Two and Hide and Seek.
exit: Which poem is about the adult remembering?
Give one short phrase and explain an effect.
Big question: how do poets use a child's view to shape feeling?
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph comparing the childhood in Piano with childhood in one other poem.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-teach childhood vocabulary and provide a sentence-stem planner. Stretch: explore how rhythm and sound recreate the memory in Piano.

lessons.title: Sonnet 116: love, time and the sonnet form
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a fourteen-line form help a poet argue that love never changes?
objectives: Analyse the structure and argument of Sonnet 116
Explain how imagery of the star and the ship shows constancy
Link form to meaning
successCriteria: All: identify the sonnet's argument
Most: analyse the sea-mark and star images
Some: explain how the volta and couplet shape the poem's final claim
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Elizabethan culture and the sonnet craze; Arabic: metre in classical Arabic poetry
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: sincere commitment; Moral: constancy and loyalty in relationships

keywords.def: a 14-line poem, in iambic pentameter
a turn in thought or argument
a line of ten syllables in five unstressed-stressed pairs
two rhyming lines closing the poem
giving human qualities to a non-human thing

starter: Bismillah. Define 'volta'.
How many lines in a sonnet?
Why might a poet make a promise in a fixed form?

teach.heading: The argument
bullets: Love is not love if it changes
True love is like a fixed mark or star
Time cannot damage true love
The couplet challenges anyone to disprove the claim
teach.note: TEACHER: supply Sonnet 116 (Shakespeare) from the anthology; it is public domain, so pupils can annotate it. The sonnet has an English (Shakespearean) rhyme scheme: ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. It is likely from the 1609 Quarto, though its exact date is not known. Use short phrases only on slides: 'ever-fixed mark', 'Love's not Time's fool'. Ask: what does the speaker claim, and why is it a bold claim? Also note the poem does not name any beloved: it is a general argument about love.

teach.heading: Two images of constancy
teach.note: Ask pupils to unpack each image. The 'ever-fixed mark' is a sea-mark such as a beacon or lighthouse that does not move in storms; the star guides ships even though its height can be measured, its true worth cannot. Contrast with the unsteady 'wandering bark' (ship). Avoid translating line by line: aim for effect.

right.title: Unsteady things
points: Love that 'alters when it alteration finds'

teach.heading: Model: form and meaning
teach.note: I do. Notice how the paragraph names the technique, quotes briefly, explains the effect on meaning and ties it to structure. Remind pupils that the final couplet is where a sonnet often delivers its bold conclusion.

model.problem: How does Shakespeare use structure to present love as constant?
steps: Point: the sonnet moves from a definition to a challenge.
Evidence: the final couplet dares the reader to prove him wrong ('If this be error').
Zoom: staking his own writing and the existence of love on his claim shows total conviction, so the form feels like a verdict.
Link: the regular iambic rhythm gives a steady, dependable beat that mirrors constancy.
model.answer: Shakespeare uses the sonnet's structure to present love as unchanging. The first twelve lines build a definition, but the closing couplet turns it into a challenge, staking the poet's own writing ('If this be error') on the claim. This total conviction, combined with the steady iambic rhythm, makes the poem's argument feel as fixed as the star it describes.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils often say 'the volta is in line 9' as if it were a rule. In an English sonnet it is often there, but also at the couplet. The key is to explain the effect.

check.q: What is the function of the final couplet?
options: It repeats the first line.
It stakes the poet's own claim on the argument and closes with certainty.
It introduces a new speaker.
It describes the ship.
check.why: The couplet delivers the emphatic conclusion. A, C and D do not match the poem.

teach.heading: Comparing with later poems
bullets: Remember (Rossetti) is also a sonnet
Compare the ideas about love and time
Compare form: English or Petrarchan
Use for AO3 links
teach.note: Preview Remember (Rossetti), a Petrarchan sonnet, which will be studied later. For now ask: why might a poet choose a sonnet to write about love? Invite predictions. This builds retrieval for the comparison lesson.

practice: Retrieve: list the four parts of a comparison paragraph.
What is iambic pentameter? Tap the rhythm of 'To be or not to be'.
Why might a poem about love use images of the sea?
independent: Core: write a paragraph on the star image using point, evidence, zoom.
Extend: write on the effect of time in the poem.
Stretch: write a short comparison plan with Remember (to be taught later).
exit: What is the main claim of the sonnet?
Name two features of its structure.
Big question: how can a fourteen-line form help a poet argue that love never changes?
lessons.homework: Learn a short phrase for each of: constancy, time, love. Write a sentence on each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a glossary of archaic words (bark, impediments) with modern meanings and a paragraph frame. Stretch: compare the claim with your own view of loyalty.

lessons.title: Romantic voices: The Tyger and La Belle Dame sans Merci
lessons.bigQuestion: How do Romantic poets use questions and stories to explore power and danger?
objectives: Analyse Blake's use of questions, rhythm and repetition in The Tyger
Analyse Keats's use of the ballad form and framing in La Belle Dame sans Merci
Compare how each poet presents a powerful, dangerous figure
successCriteria: All: identify one technique in each poem
Most: explain effects of rhetorical questions and ballad structure
Some: compare how both poems leave the reader uneasy
lessons.crossCurricular: Art: Blake's illuminated printing; History: the Industrial Revolution and the Romantic reaction
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: awe at creation and the limits of human understanding; Moral: temptation and responsibility

keywords.def: a question asked for effect, not for an answer
a story told in short, usually four-line, stanzas
a rhythm of stressed then unstressed syllables
relating to a period valuing emotion, nature and imagination
a repeated line or phrase

starter: Bismillah. Define 'rhetorical question' and give an effect it can have.
Name two features of a ballad.
What is AO3 and how do you earn it?

teach.heading: The Tyger: questions about a creator
bullets: Songs of Experience, 1794
Every stanza but the last is questions
The speaker wonders who could create such a creature
Contrast with the Lamb of Songs of Innocence
teach.note: TEACHER: supply The Tyger (William Blake) from the licensed anthology. The poem is six quatrains with strong, hammering rhythm and rhyming couplets. Key reading: the speaker asks what kind of maker could 'frame' something so fearsome ('fearful symmetry'), and whether the same creator made the Lamb. The blacksmith imagery of hammer, chain, furnace and anvil makes creation sound like hard, violent labour. The last stanza repeats the first with 'dare' replacing 'could', which raises the stakes. Context: Blake lived through the early Industrial Revolution and was critical of power and of institutions; do not overclaim a single reading, because critics differ.

teach.heading: Model: questions and rhythm
teach.note: I do. Highlight that the paragraph names the technique, quotes a short phrase, then zooms on one word and gives an effect. Ask pupils to hear the beat by tapping the rhythm.

model.problem: How does Blake create awe and fear in The Tyger?
steps: Point: he uses a barrage of unanswered questions.
Evidence: 'What immortal hand or eye' and later the blacksmith's 'anvil'.
Zoom: the questions give no answers, so the creator stays mysterious and frightening; the industrial image of an anvil makes creation sound violent.
Link: the changed final line 'dare' turns curiosity into fear.
model.answer: Blake creates awe and fear through a barrage of unanswered questions. By asking what 'immortal hand or eye' could make the tiger, he leaves the creator mysterious, and the blacksmith's 'anvil' makes creation sound like violent labour. The final stanza's 'dare' in place of 'could' intensifies the speaker's sense that to create such a being is dangerous.

teach.heading: La Belle Dame sans Merci: a ballad of enchantment
bullets: Written 1819 by John Keats
A knight is found alone and pale
He tells of a 'faery's child' who enchants him
Ends where it began: cold, bare and lonely
teach.note: TEACHER: supply La Belle Dame sans Merci (John Keats) from the licensed anthology. The poem uses short four-line stanzas with a shortened final line, a pattern typical of the traditional ballad. It opens with a questioner who finds the knight; the knight then tells his story, so the poem has a frame. Ask: why might the final stanza return to the opening image ('Alone and palely loitering')? The title is French for 'the beautiful lady without mercy'. Keats's other 'victims' appear in a dream as pale kings and warriors. Caution: do not claim certainty about the figure's nature; the poem's ambiguity is the point.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils often claim the lady is simply 'evil'. The poem deliberately leaves her nature ambiguous: is she a seductress, a faery, or a projection of the knight's desire? Encourage tentative language like 'suggests' and 'perhaps'.

check.q: What is the effect of Keats's ending, which returns to the knight alone?
options: It shows the story was a lie.
It creates a cyclical, haunting structure and leaves the knight trapped in his loss.
It introduces a new character.
It shows the knight is happy.
check.why: The echo of the opening makes the poem circular: the knight is stuck. A, C and D are not supported by the text.

teach.heading: Comparing the two
teach.note: Use the compare block as a plan for the AO3 link. Ask pupils to find one shared idea (power that charms and endangers) and one contrast (Blake interrogates a creator; Keats narrates a victim's experience).

right.title: La Belle Dame sans Merci
points: Ballad stanza with a short final line

practice: Retrieve: why do poets use rhyme? Give two effects.
What does 'Romantic' mean in literary terms?
Say a line of any poem you know aloud and tap its rhythm.
independent: Core: write a paragraph on one technique in The Tyger.
Extend: write a paragraph on the effect of the ballad frame in Keats.
Stretch: write a comparison paragraph linking the two poems through danger and power.
exit: Name one technique in each poem.
Write one linking sentence with 'whereas'.
Big question: how do Romantic poets use questions and stories to explore power and danger?
lessons.homework: Write a comparison paragraph (about 120 words) on how the creature or lady is presented. Use two short quotations.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-teach archaic vocabulary (thee, thy, loitering, sedge) and give sentence stems. Stretch: read the poems alongside Blake's Lamb or Keats's context and consider why critics disagree.

lessons.title: My Last Duchess: power, control and the dramatic monologue
lessons.bigQuestion: How does Browning let a speaker condemn himself with his own words?
objectives: Explain what a dramatic monologue is
Analyse how the Duke reveals his character through language and form
Link the poem to its Renaissance setting without bolting on facts
successCriteria: All: identify the speaker and listener
Most: analyse an example of control in the Duke's words
Some: explain how enjambment and rhyme create a mask of calm
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Renaissance Italy and patronage; Drama: voice and persona
lessons.smsc: Moral: abuse of power and respect for the dignity of every person; Social: how marriage should be built on kindness (mawaddah and rahmah)

keywords.def: a poem in which a character speaks to a silent listener, revealing themselves
a sentence running over a line break
a ten-syllable line with an unstressed-stressed pattern
a character created by the writer
meaning the opposite of what is said, or readers knowing more than a speaker

starter: Bismillah. What does 'persona' mean?
Define enjambment and give an effect it can have.
Why can a speaker be unreliable?

teach.heading: A speaker and a silent listener
bullets: Browning, 1842
Duke of Ferrara speaks to an envoy
He is arranging a new marriage
He shows a portrait of his 'last' wife
teach.note: TEACHER: supply My Last Duchess (Robert Browning) from the licensed anthology. Browning based the poem loosely on a real Duke of Ferrara, but the characters and speech are his invention; do not treat it as a documentary account. The listener never speaks, so we hear everything through the Duke. Ask: what does the opening 'That's my last Duchess painted on the wall' suggest about how he sees her? (She is an object, 'my' possession.) Explain the context in one sentence: Renaissance rulers treated marriage as a political alliance, and Browning exposes the arrogance such power could breed.

teach.heading: Control hidden in couplets
teach.note: The poem is rhyming couplets in iambic pentameter, but the sentences run over the line ends (enjambment), so the rhyme barely shows. This creates the sound of calm, casual conversation while the content is chilling. Ask pupils to read two lines aloud and notice how quickly the rhyme can vanish. This is a form point they must be able to explain.

left.title: What the Duke says
points: Treats the portrait as a prized object

right.title: What we learn
points: He resented her kindness to others
'I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together'

teach.heading: Model: the Duke's possessiveness
teach.note: I do. Note that the paragraph quotes, then deduces character from the word choice. Stress that the Duke condemns himself, so the poem's irony is that the reader sees what he cannot.

model.problem: How does Browning present the Duke as controlling?
steps: Point: he presents the Duke as a man who sees people as possessions.
Evidence: he says 'my last Duchess' and shows her as a painting that only he may reveal.
Zoom: the possessive 'my' and the curtain only he draws show he controls even her image, and 'I gave commands' suggests he removed her freedom.
Link: the casual enjambed couplets make the cruelty sound like a polite chat.
model.answer: Browning presents the Duke as a man who treats people as possessions. By calling her 'my last Duchess' and keeping her portrait behind a curtain that only he opens, the Duke shows that he wants to control even her image. The casual, enjambed couplets make his cruelty sound like polite conversation, which makes the reader recoil all the more.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Ask pupils to justify their choice with a short quotation. Common misconception: that the poem is about the Duchess. It is about the Duke's character as revealed by what he says.

check.q: What is the best reading of 'I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together'?
options: The Duke gave orders and she stopped smiling because she was sad.
The Duke implies he removed her, and the cold tone hides the horror.
The Duke dismissed a servant.
The Duke is describing a painting.
check.why: The phrase is deliberately ambiguous and chilling: the casual tone hides the implication that he had her silenced or killed. Other options do not account for the ominous tone.

teach.heading: The ending
bullets: He mentions a bronze of Neptune taming a sea-horse
Neptune subdues an animal: a symbol of the Duke himself
The poem ends on art, not people
What does this say about his priorities?
teach.note: Ask: why end on a sculpture? The Duke's final pride in the bronze shows that he sees people, objects and art as possessions to be controlled. Contrast with the Duchess's warmth. A good AO2 point: the ending returns to the language of art and ownership, so the structure supports the character.

practice: Retrieve: what is the difference between narrator and persona?
Why might a poet use rhyming couplets for a controlling character?
What is irony? Give a quick everyday example.
independent: Core: write a paragraph on the Duke's possessiveness using the model.
Extend: write a paragraph on how enjambment disguises the rhyme.
Stretch: plan a comparison of the Duke's voice with the speaker's voice in If-.
exit: Who speaks and who listens?
Name one form feature and its effect.
Big question: how does Browning let a speaker condemn himself?
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph (about 100 words) on the Duke's attitude to women, with two short quotations.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a paraphrase of difficult sentences and a glossary (envoy, countenance, dowry). Stretch: explore how the monologue's silent listener invites the reader to judge.

lessons.title: War Photographer: witness, memory and indifference
lessons.bigQuestion: Who is responsible for what we see of other people's suffering?
objectives: Analyse how Duffy presents the photographer's work and emotions
Explain the effect of the darkroom and church imagery
Link the poem's structure to the move from conflict to comfortable homes
successCriteria: All: summarise what happens in each stanza
Most: analyse two images
Some: evaluate who the poem criticises
lessons.crossCurricular: Art/Media: photojournalism and ethics; History: late 20th-century conflicts
lessons.smsc: Moral: duty to witness and to help; Social: compassion fatigue

keywords.def: placing two contrasting ideas side by side
a group of words linked by meaning
when what is said or done contrasts with what is expected
a group of lines in a poem
a claim that someone has done wrong

starter: Bismillah. What is juxtaposition? Give a brief example.
Name a semantic field linked to church.
Why might a poet use regular stanzas to describe a disturbing subject?

teach.heading: The photographer in the darkroom
bullets: Duffy, a contemporary British poet
He develops photographs of war zones
Places named include Ulster (Northern Ireland), Beirut and Phnom Penh
He is back in England, 'finally alone'
teach.note: TEACHER: supply War Photographer (Carol Ann Duffy) from the licensed anthology. The poem has four six-line stanzas with a regular rhyme scheme. The photographer works in a red-lit darkroom: the poem compares this to a church and a priest at Mass, which suggests his work is solemn, almost holy. Explain the place references: Ulster (Northern Ireland during the Troubles), Beirut (the Lebanese civil war) and Phnom Penh (Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge). Without being gruesome, say that the poem asks about the viewer's response.

teach.heading: Two worlds side by side
teach.note: Pupils contrast the photographer's memories of conflict with the 'rural England' to which he returns and the newspaper readers' brief tears. The structural point: the poem moves from a quiet darkroom to the horrifying images, to comfortable readers, which makes us ask whether we are guilty of indifference.

left.title: The war zones
points: A man's final moments as the image develops
Grief of a woman who cannot be comforted

teach.heading: Model: church imagery
teach.note: I do. Notice the paragraph links a single image to the poem's argument. Ask: what would change if the darkroom was compared to a laboratory instead?

model.problem: How does Duffy present the photographer's work as important?
steps: Point: she uses religious imagery to make his work seem sacred.
Evidence: the red light, and the idea of a priest preparing to say Mass.
Zoom: comparing a darkroom to a church gives him a solemn duty and suggests that the victims deserve reverence.
Link: the contrast with readers who finish their tears 'between the bath and pre-lunch beers' accuses the public of treating suffering lightly.
model.answer: Duffy presents the photographer's work as sacred by comparing his darkroom to a church and the photographer to a priest. This religious imagery gives his work a solemn duty and suggests that the victims deserve reverence, which makes the readers' brief tears, shed 'between the bath and pre-lunch beers', seem shallow by contrast.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Discuss the distractors. B is tempting but too narrow. The poem criticises not only editors and readers; it also asks what the photographer feels.

check.q: Who does the poem most clearly criticise?
options: The war photographer for taking pictures.
A comfortable public who see suffering and quickly move on.
The victims.
The poet's own village.
check.why: The final stanza draws attention to readers' short-lived sympathy. The photographer is presented sympathetically; the victims are not criticised.

teach.heading: Form and ending
bullets: Regular stanzas and rhyme: control, order
Controlled form versus chaotic subject
The ending: he does 'what someone must'
Ask: is the ending hopeful or bitter?
teach.note: Ask pupils to consider the tension between the neat form and the horror. A regular pattern can show the photographer's effort to keep control. Invite a balanced view of the ending: the photographer carries the burden while others look away.

practice: Retrieve: what is a semantic field?
Name two effects of regular rhyme.
What does 'witness' mean?
independent: Core: write a paragraph on the church imagery.
Extend: write a paragraph on the effect of the final stanza.
Stretch: plan a comparison with Prayer Before Birth on how each poet presents suffering.
exit: Name one image and its effect.
Who does the poem blame?
Big question: who is responsible for what we see of others' suffering?
lessons.homework: Write a comparison paragraph on suffering in War Photographer and one other poem you have studied.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: avoid graphic detail; give a labelled list of place names and a visual of a darkroom. Stretch: research ethical codes for photojournalists.

lessons.title: Half-caste: voice, performance and identity
lessons.bigQuestion: How can the form of a poem challenge the way people are labelled?
objectives: Analyse how Agard uses non-standard spelling, humour and direct address
Explain how the poem challenges the term 'half-caste'
Compare Half-caste with Search For My Tongue
successCriteria: All: identify the poem's attitude to the term 'half-caste'
Most: analyse the effect of non-standard language
Some: compare two poets' methods of presenting identity
lessons.crossCurricular: Arabic: language, accent and identity; Art: examples Agard uses (such as Picasso)
lessons.smsc: Moral: dignity of all people (karamah); Spiritual: Surah al-Hujurat 49:13, that humanity was made into peoples and tribes to know one another

keywords.def: language that departs from the standard written form, such as dialect or Creole
a language formed from a mix of languages, spoken in the Caribbean and elsewhere
speaking straight to the reader or listener
poetry written to be spoken aloud
a fixed and unfair idea about a group

starter: Bismillah. What is the effect of direct address?
Define 'dialect'.
Which technique did Bhatt use to show identity in her poem?

teach.heading: A sensitive and important poem
bullets: John Agard, born in Guyana, moved to Britain in 1977
The poem targets the term 'half-caste'
Agard writes in Creole-influenced spelling
The speaker argues each person is whole
teach.note: TEACHER: supply Half-caste (John Agard) from the licensed anthology. 'Half-caste' is an outdated and offensive term; it appears only because the poem challenges it. Remind pupils to use the word only when quoting and analysing, and to treat the topic with respect. Remind them that this is a poem about dignity: link to the Qur'anic idea (Surah al-Hujurat 49:13) that human diversity exists so people may know one another, and that nobility lies in righteousness, not appearance. Agard is a Guyanese-born poet and performer; the poem is meant to be performed.

teach.heading: Voice, spelling and humour
teach.note: The speaker uses everyday examples (such as art and music) to show that mixing makes something richer, not lesser. Ask pupils how the Creole-influenced spelling ('yu', 'wha', 'mih') changes how we hear the poem and who the speaker is. Ask: what is the tone: angry, playful, or both?

right.title: What he argues
points: A person is a whole human being

teach.heading: Model: language as resistance
teach.note: I do. Notice how the paragraph links the spelling to the speaker's cultural identity, and then to the poem's argument. Ask pupils to read the phrase aloud in the voice of the poem.

model.problem: How does Agard use language to challenge prejudice in Half-caste?
steps: Point: he uses non-standard spelling to give the speaker a confident, distinct voice.
Evidence: the demand 'Explain yuself'.
Zoom: the imperative and the Creole-influenced spelling put the speaker in charge and force the listener to justify the label.
Link: the poem shows that a language form can be as valid as standard English.
model.answer: Agard gives the speaker a confident voice through non-standard spelling. The demand 'Explain yuself' is an imperative, which makes the speaker, not the listener, the one in control, while the spelling asserts that this way of speaking is valid. The language form is therefore part of the poem's argument against prejudice.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Discuss why D is wrong: the humour is part of the argument. The poem is playful but serious.

check.q: Why does Agard end by inviting the listener to return with 'de whole of yu eye'?
options: To be polite.
To suggest that to understand someone you must give them your whole attention and respect.
To say that the speaker will leave.
To make the poem rhyme.
check.why: The ending turns the poem's argument back on the listener: they must see whole people. The other options do not fit the tone or meaning.

teach.heading: Compare: Half-caste and Search For My Tongue
bullets: Both explore language and identity
Agard: confrontational and performed
Bhatt: reflective and personal
Both let language appear on the page as itself
teach.note: Plan a quick AO3 link. Pupils find one similarity (language as identity) and one difference (public argument versus private journey). Remind them to link methods as well as ideas.

practice: Retrieve: define 'direct address'.
Name two features of a dramatic monologue.
What is a stereotype?
independent: Core: write a paragraph on the effect of non-standard spelling.
Extend: write a paragraph on how Agard uses examples.
Stretch: write a comparison paragraph between Half-caste and Search For My Tongue.
exit: What does the poem argue?
Name one method and its effect.
Big question: how can a poem's form challenge the way people are labelled?
lessons.homework: Write a comparison paragraph (about 120 words) on identity in Half-caste and Search For My Tongue.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-teach the word 'caste' and 'dialect' with sensitivity; provide the model's sentence frames. EAL pupils may share how accents and languages feel in their own lives. Stretch: research performance poetry and compare the written and spoken versions.

lessons.title: Death and memory: Do not go gentle, Remember and Poem at Thirty-Nine
lessons.bigQuestion: How do poets speak to someone they will lose, and what do they want from them?
objectives: Analyse the villanelle form of Do not go gentle into that good night
Analyse the Petrarchan structure of Remember
Apply the method to Poem at Thirty-Nine and compare the three
successCriteria: All: identify who speaks to whom in each poem
Most: analyse form in two poems
Some: compare the speakers' requests
lessons.crossCurricular: Islamic Studies: remembering the dead and du'a; History: Victorian attitudes to mourning
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: remembrance of the deceased and making du'a; Moral: honouring parents

keywords.def: a 19-line poem with two repeating refrains
a repeated line
a 14-line poem of an octave and a sestet
the first eight lines of a Petrarchan sonnet
the final six lines of a Petrarchan sonnet

starter: Bismillah. What is a volta?
What two parts form a Petrarchan sonnet?
Name a poem in the anthology addressed to a loved one.

teach.heading: Do not go gentle: a son's command
bullets: Dylan Thomas, 1951
A villanelle: two refrains repeat
The speaker urges a dying father to resist
Wise, good, wild and grave men all resist
teach.note: TEACHER: supply Do not go gentle into that good night (Dylan Thomas). The poem was written for Thomas's dying father. The villanelle form, with its two repeating lines, makes the plea sound like an obsessive, desperate chant. The refrain 'Rage, rage against the dying of the light' is the emotional peak. The poem ends on a direct plea for his father's 'fierce tears'. Ask: what does the speaker want his father to do, and why? Note that the speaker commands but also begs.

teach.heading: Remember: a gentle request
teach.note: Remember (Christina Rossetti) is a Petrarchan sonnet: the octave asks to be remembered, the sestet turns ('Yet if you should forget me for a while') and says that it is better to forget and smile than to remember and be sad. Compare tone: Thomas demands, Rossetti permits. Ask pupils to say which request is more selfless and why. Context: Rossetti wrote the poem as a young woman; she was a devout Anglican and wrote often about love and death. Do not guess at biography beyond this.

left.title: Do not go gentle
points: Speaker fears loss and wants resistance

right.title: Remember
points: Gentle request, then permission to forget
Speaker values the loved one's happiness

teach.heading: Model: contrasting requests
teach.note: I do. Show how a link sentence can use a pair of quotations. Ask: which poem would comfort a mourner more?

model.problem: Compare how each speaker addresses the person they will lose.
steps: Point: both speakers address a loved one, but make opposite requests.
Evidence: Thomas demands 'Rage, rage', Rossetti allows 'forget and smile'.
Zoom: the repeated imperative creates urgency and defiance, while the gentle permission shows selfless love.
Link: the villanelle's repetition suits the first, whereas the sonnet's turn suits the second.
model.answer: Both speakers address a loved one but make opposite requests. Thomas commands 'Rage, rage', and the repeated imperative creates urgent defiance, whereas Rossetti's speaker permits the listener to 'forget and smile', which reveals a selfless love. The villanelle's insistent refrains suit Thomas's desperation, but the sonnet's turn allows Rossetti's gentle change of heart.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Use the quick vote. The common error is B: the poem is addressed to the father, not a general reader.

check.q: Why does Thomas use a villanelle?
options: Because villanelles are about death.
The repeating refrains create an obsessive, pleading chant that suits his desperate plea.
To show he is a wise man.
Because the poem is about nature.
check.why: The repetition mirrors his refusal to let go. A is untrue as a rule; C and D do not account for the form's effect.

teach.heading: Poem at Thirty-Nine: apply the method
bullets: Alice Walker, an American poet and novelist
A speaker reflects on her father
Ask: who speaks, to whom, in what form?
Teacher supplies the text
teach.note: TEACHER: supply Poem at Thirty-Nine (Alice Walker) from the licensed anthology; do not rely on memory of its details. This is a method slide: have pupils annotate voice, address, tone, structure and what the speaker learns about her father and herself. Then compare to Do not go gentle and Remember: all three poems are about family or love and loss. Ask: does the speaker seem to be accepting, resisting, or rediscovering?

practice: Retrieve: define 'refrain' and 'octave'.
Which poem so far has an unusual rhyme scheme and why?
What do du'a for the deceased remind us about remembrance?
independent: Core: write a paragraph on the villanelle form.
Extend: write a paragraph on the volta in Remember.
Stretch: write a three-way comparison plan (Thomas, Rossetti, Walker) of how each poet addresses loss.
exit: Name the form of Remember.
What does the refrain in Thomas's poem do?
Big question: how do poets speak to someone they will lose?
lessons.homework: Write a comparison paragraph (about 120 words) on the tone of Do not go gentle and Remember.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a form map (villanelle and sonnet) with colour-coded refrains. EAL pupils can add their own family terms. Stretch: compare with a favourite elegy from your own reading.

objectives: Plan a Section B comparison in five minutes
Write a comparative introduction and body paragraph
Use timing and a checklist

keywords.def: dealing with two or more things by setting them against each other
a word that links ideas
the central argument of an essay

a short quotation woven into a sentence

starter: Bismillah. List the four parts of a comparison paragraph.
Which two AOs does Section B assess?

teach.heading: The question and the clock
bullets: 30 marks, about 40 minutes
A choice of two questions
Read both, then choose carefully
5 minutes plan, 30 writing, 5 checking
teach.note: Remind pupils the exam supplies a clean copy of the poems. Check the latest past papers or specimen paper for the precise stems and the AO2/AO3 split, which was not confirmed when this scheme was written. An example (original) question for practice: 'Compare how poets present the effects of time on people in Remember and one other poem from Part 3 of the anthology.' Ask pupils how they would choose the second poem: one that offers strong links in theme and contrasting methods.

teach.heading: The plan: a comparison grid
teach.note: Teach a grid of three rows (idea/theme, methods, effect) and two columns (poem A, poem B). Pupils fill it with short quotations. The point of the plan is to prevent writing two separate essays. Use the table as a template and show a filled example.

teach.heading: Model: introduction and linked paragraph
teach.note: I do. Read the answer aloud. Point out the thesis in the introduction, the comparing connective, and the short quotations embedded in sentences. Ask: where is AO2? Where is AO3?

model.problem: Compare how poets present the effects of time on people in Remember and one other poem.
steps: Introduction: state a clear comparison thesis in one or two sentences.
Paragraph: point, linked evidence from both poems.
Zoom: explain a language or form feature in each.
Link: end with a judgement about contrasting attitudes.
model.answer: Rossetti and Thomas both present time as a force that takes loved ones, but respond differently. In Remember, the gentle 'forget and smile' accepts the passing of time peacefully, whereas Thomas's commanding 'Rage, rage' refuses to accept it. The sonnet's turn shows Rossetti's gradual acceptance, while the villanelle's refrains trap Thomas in his defiance.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Ask pupils to rank A to D from weakest to strongest. A and C separate poems; D has a vague claim.

check.q: Which opening sentence is strongest for a comparison?
options: Remember is a sonnet by Rossetti.
Rossetti accepts loss gently, whereas Thomas fights it fiercely.
Both poems are about death.
Poets use many techniques.
check.why: B states a clear comparison with both poets. A is a single-poem fact, C is too general, D has no content.

teach.heading: Checklist for marks
bullets: Short quotations embedded in sentences
Methods named and explained
Links every paragraph, not only at the end
Conclude with a judgement
teach.note: Give a checklist for self-assessment. Remind pupils that AO3 is about connections, so each paragraph should link the poems, not just the conclusion. If time allows, pupils peer-mark a paragraph with two stars and a wish.

practice: Retrieve: three connectives for similarity and three for contrast.
Write one embedded quotation from any poem you know.
What is the danger of writing about poem A for half and then poem B?
independent: Core: complete a comparison grid for the practice question.
Extend: write the introduction and one body paragraph.
Stretch: write a conclusion that makes a judgement.
exit: How many minutes for planning?
Write one linking sentence.
Big question: how do you turn knowledge into a comparative essay?

lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide the grid pre-filled with prompts and a word bank of connectives. Extra time and a scribe if needed. Stretch: pupils write under timed conditions and self-assess against the checklist.

Spot language, form and structure features and explain their effects
Write one analytical paragraph on an unseen poem

language that creates pictures or sensations
the writer's attitude or mood
how a poem is organised from start to end
